Ph.D. Candidate in Industrial and Systems Engineering


Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering · University at Buffalo


My research combines causal inference, machine learning, and operations research to support treatment and care decisions. I am particularly interested in learning how interventions affect outcomes from observational data and determining when additional evidence would improve a decision.
Much of my doctoral work concerns aging and caregiving, with particular attention to how caregiver burden affects older adults’ transitions into long-term care. A complementary part of my research concerns sequential experimentation, where the challenge is to identify the best options while making efficient use of costly comparisons. I plan to extend these efforts to personalized treatment selection and medical technologies that adapt to patients’ changing conditions
In teaching, I emphasize the reasoning behind an engineering model: what it represents, which assumptions it relies on, and what conclusions it can support. Through case exercises and peer discussion, I give students opportunities to explain their choices, consider alternative approaches, and revise their work. My goal is to help them develop the understanding and independent judgment needed to address unfamiliar problems, including those involving AI recommendations.
My research has appeared in IISE Transactions and Quality and Reliability Engineering International. I received the 2025–2026 University at Buffalo ISE Graduate Student Teaching Award and was selected as an IISE Future Faculty Fellow.

My research brings together operations research, machine learning, and observational data analysis, with applications primarily in healthcare. Within this domain, I work on causal effect estimation and sequential experimentation: determining what can be learned about intervention effects from existing data, and which additional evaluations would best inform a treatment or care decision.


My doctoral research develops adversarial balancing representations for dose–response estimation, with particular attention to caregiver burden and older adults’ transitions into long-term care. Here, the methodological task is to reduce measured differences across exposure levels while preserving the information needed for outcome estimation.
The caregiver focus emerged from my systematic review of dementia-management research, which identified limited attention to caregiver circumstances alongside weaknesses in confounding adjustment. In conducting this review, I applied PSM-Qual, a rubric I co-developed to assess propensity-score implementation. My related work on caregiving measurement led to the development of CareBI, in which burden and benefit are represented as separate dimensions.



My first-authored paper in IISE Transactions addresses a problem that arose in crowdlearning: how to assign pairwise comparisons so that the best student-created materials can be identified with limited evaluation effort. I led the development of a sequential experimentation methodology that prioritizes comparisons by their expected contribution to subset selection. Its computational component uses Markov chain perturbation analysis to approximate ranking-score changes, with bounds linking these approximation errors to errors in the estimated value of additional comparisons.



I plan to extend these methodological efforts to personalized treatment selection and adaptive medical technologies, beginning with insulin delivery for older adults with type 1 diabetes. Here, previous doses influence glucose levels, which then affect subsequent dosing decisions and treatment responses. My planned work will account for these treatment histories and patient–caregiver circumstances in causal estimation, while using sequential experimentation to allocate simulation effort among dosing rules and patient scenarios. The objective is to reduce the evaluations required for treatment selection while preserving selection accuracy.

I believe good teaching begins with listening to how students reason and designing activities that make that reasoning visible. In Simulation Modeling and Analysis, I have led recitations and course lectures and developed case-based exercises using Arena and @RISK in which students define systems, identify sources of uncertainty, make modeling choices, and explain what their results do and do not justify. These contributions, together with my broader work in the course, were recognized with the University at Buffalo ISE Graduate Student Teaching Award.
